title: ‘Emomee,’ Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
An Indian children’s entertainment company has brought its debut original animated series to Netflix.

	“Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis,”
body:
An Indian children’s entertainment company has brought its debut original animated series to Netflix.

	“Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis,” from the Mumbai-based brand Emomee, features 20 episodes of some 11 minutes each, centered on characters E, Mo and Mee as they navigate everyday adventures designed to build confidence, curiosity, kindness, emotional intelligence and problem-solving in preschool-age viewers.


	“This launch represents much more than a new distribution platform. It is another milestone in building Emomee into a global entertainment company. Every step we’ve taken – from growing a loyal audience to expanding onto streaming platforms – is helping us build a long-term franchise that will extend beyond content into consumer products, licensing and live experiences,” said Pooja Jauhari, founder and CEO of Emomee.
	

	Founded by Jauhari, a former CEO of WPP-acquired creative agency The Glitch, and Varun Duggirala, co-founder of The Glitch, Emomee reached one billion views across more than 100 countries and built a subscriber base of 2.5 million within 15 months of launch. The company drew further attention on “Shark Tank India,” where all five sharks made offers at the founders’ asking valuation of INR50 crore ($5.2 million). Suraksha Subramaniam rounds out the founding team, overseeing legal and IP compliance.

	Emomee has positioned itself around what it describes as a “life-skills-first” approach to children’s content, in contrast to the algorithm-driven, high-stimulation formats that have drawn scrutiny from parents and educators globally. 
	

	The Netflix debut is part of a broader expansion push that spans consumer products, licensing and live experiences. Emomee plans to attend Mipcom later this year to pursue new deals across distribution and licensing.

title: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Stays on Top as ‘V’ Debuts in Second
description: Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” held onto the No. 1 position at the mainland China box office during the Aug.
body:
Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” held onto the No. 1 position at the mainland China box office during the Aug. 21–23 weekend, taking in RMB298.8 million ($43.9 million) in its second weekend of release, according to data from Artisan Gateway. 

	Directed by Wen Muye (“Dying to Survive”) and starring Shen Teng, Jiang Qiming, Aarif Rahman, and Omar Sherif, the hit production has accumulated $232.2 million since launching nationwide on Aug. 11. The story tracks a Chinese chef who moves to the Middle East to clear family debts by running a restaurant, only to see the venue become a community refuge when armed conflict breaks out across the region.
	

	Pearl River Film Group’s crime drama “V” debuted in second place, pulling in $18.9 million over the three-day weekend frame. Bolstered by early screenings following its Aug. 19 premiere, the feature has reached a cumulative total of $30.7 million. Directed by Han Yan (“Love Never Ends”), the film features a heavyweight ensemble cast led by Tony Ka Fai Leung, Zhu Yilong, Tan Jianci, and Kara Wai. The narrative follows an ambitious figure who uses relentless daring and sharp enterprise to rise through the ranks and taste immense success, only to see dark consequences and long-buried shadows gather to threaten his triumph.


	Universal’s epic “The Odyssey” took third position in its sophomore frame, collecting $15.9 million for a total of $68.7 million. 

	Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy feature “All Wishes Come True!” moved to fourth place in its sixth weekend, adding $9.8 million. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the enduring family hit has amassed $255.7 million since its July 18 debut.
	

	Sony’s superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” rounded out the top five, generating $4.6 million in its fourth full weekend, lifting its cumulative total in China to $219.9 million since rolling out on July 29.

	Mainland China’s overall weekend grosses reached $103.1 million, while the 2026 year-to-date revenue stands at $4 billion, down 28.6% from the same period in 2025.

schema.headline: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Stays on Top as ‘V’ Debuts in Second

title: Busan Unveils 23-Film Vision Section Lineup
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled 23 Korean and Asian independent films for its Vision section, split into 12 titles un
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled 23 Korean and Asian independent films for its Vision section, split into 12 titles under Vision-Korea and 11 under Vision-Asia.

	The Vision section grew out of Korean Cinema Today – Vision, expanding last year into a standalone program covering filmmakers across the continent. This year’s lineup pairs established names still building out distinctive bodies of work with emerging talents who have begun drawing international notice, and it comes with 10 Vision-Asia awards and nine Vision-Korea awards recognizing achievement across a range of categories.
	

	Several Vision-Korea filmmakers return to Busan with festival history behind them. Kim Miyoung, whose “A Lonely Island in the Distant Sea” (2023) won the DGK Megabox Award at BIFF, brings “Some Detective.” Park Songyeol, a past winner of the Critic b Award and the KBS Independent Film Award for “Hot in Day, Cold at Night,” explores family and mortality in “Beyond Love’s Horizon.” Sohn Hyun-lok, whose debut “That Summer’s Lie” took the Fipresci Prize at BIFF in 2023, follows a string of student fall accidents in “The Birds.” Jang Woojin, recognized previously at BIFF and at the Berlin Film Festival, examines love, loss and chance in “Cosmic Trace.” Park Hong-min, whose work has drawn attention from BIFF, the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the Vancouver International Film Festival, continues his recurring cinematic world in “Space.”


	The rest of the Vision-Korea slate mixes newer voices with directors making the leap to features. Kim Hyomi makes her animated feature debut with “Earbug,” about an aspiring novelist confronting her own trauma. Park Kun-young, previously behind “To My River” and “A Distance Place,” presents “Things I Left at the Theater.” Shin Dongmin’s “Not For You” traces two brothers reuniting a decade after their father’s departure, while Oh Sehyeon’s “Baler,” a follow-up to 2022’s “Usu,” follows a woman’s month working a seasonal farm job. Shin Sun returns with “Nothing Has Happened Yet” after “No Surprise” and “Maze.” Jeong Jihye’s “Full Moon” follows a girl hiding her parents from public view, and Kim Si-jin makes his first feature with the animated “The Flower,” centered on an aging crematorium director. Both “Not For You” and “Some Detective” made this year’s Asian Cinema Fund fund for films in post-production.
	

	Vision-Asia brings together directors from 10 countries and regions. Vietnam’s Nguyễn Hoàng Điệp presents “1982,” following a filmmaker’s search for a missing parent. Japan’s Kumamoto Ryohei, working from a background in commercials and music videos, makes his feature debut with “After the Song.” Hong Kong’s Isabella Lam Lok-hin debuts with “Dead End,” centered on a man confronting long-buried family history. The Philippines’ Arvin Belarmino presents “Ria,” about a folk-punk musician fighting to hold onto his music and home. Mongolia’s Sakhya Byamba, who took the New Currents prize at Busan in 2013 for “Remote Control,” returns with the satirical “Zogsool.”

	The remaining Vision-Asia selections include Iran’s Mani Moghaddam, whose feature debut “Slumber” uses magical realism to address the country’s oppressive realities, and Thailand’s “Bua,” the directorial debut of actor Inthira Charoenpura alongside co-director Phensiri Klangsurin. India is represented twice, with Sailesh Rathnakumar’s debut “Selvi,” produced by and starring acclaimed actor Anjali Patil, and Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark,” the latter from a filmmaker previously known for writing and cinematography work with outlets including Netflix. Kazakhstan’s Darkhan Tulegenov presents “The Cord,” about a mother fighting to prove her son’s innocence, and Japan’s Yaza Takenoshin, who first drew attention at 16 with a documentary on nuclear power, makes his feature debut with “Hinotama: Ball of Fire.”

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Outmuscles ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ to Hold Top Spot
description:
“The Odyssey” maintained its commanding position atop the South Korea box office during the weekend of Aug. 21–23. 

	According to data from KOBIS,
body:
“The Odyssey” maintained its commanding position atop the South Korea box office during the weekend of Aug. 21–23. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Christopher Nolan-directed tentpole generated $10.6 million from 1,321,204 admissions over the three-day frame across 2,182 screens, capturing 66.3% of total weekend business. Showing formidable holding power in its third outing, the film pushed its cumulative local gross to $56.8 million from 7,109,368 total admissions since its Aug. 5 launch.
	

	Superhero tentpole “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” held onto second place in its fourth frame, taking $2.9 million from 386,754 admissions. The film accounted for 18.39% of the market, lifting its cumulative South Korea haul to $61.4 million from 8,127,615 total admissions.


	“Insidious: Out of the Further” opened in third place, generating $547,555 from 71,592 admissions across 678 screens. Since its Aug. 20 premiere, the release has collected $706,508 from 93,922 total admissions.

	Local animated feature “Teenieping: Legend of the Whale Heartstone” finished fourth, adding $480,487 from 69,482 admissions. Directed by Kim Soo-hoon, the musical fantasy adventure follows Princess Romi, Heartsping, and their crew venturing into the deep sea to rescue Queen Velita. The sequel has grossed $5.3 million from 788,263 viewers since its Aug. 5 rollout.

	Animated mystery “Detective Conan the Movie: Fallen Angel of the Highway” took fifth place in its second weekend, pulling in $380,240 from 50,053 admissions. Directed by Takahiro Hasui, the franchise installment has reached a total of $2.5 million from 356,276 tickets.
	

	The local action-comedy sequel “Ok! Madam: Bon Voyage” took sixth place, generating $239,231 from 33,585 admissions. Directed by Lee Cheol-ha and starring Uhm Jung-hwa, Park Sung-woong, Lee Sang-yun, and Sooyoung, the film has now earned $2 million. 

	“Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie” placed seventh, collecting $143,937 from 20,488 admissions to move its gross to $671,567 from 95,605 admissions.

	Sci-fi thriller “Hope” took eighth place, adding $130,477 from 18,366 admissions. Directed by Na Hong-Jin and starring Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung, Jung Ho-yeon, Michael Fassbender, and Alicia Vikander, the alien-encounter feature has accumulated $35 million from 4,518,395 admissions.

	Studio Ghibli’s 2010 animated fantasy “The Secret World of Arrietty,” directed by Yonebayashi Hiromasa, placed ninth via a specialty re-release, earning $82,305 from 10,431 admissions to lift its lifetime South Korea gross to $5.6 million from 1,086,258 tickets.

	Rounding out the top ten was “Warfare,” which pulled in $58,172 from 7,333 admissions over the frame. The real-time Iraq War encounter film has generated $108,585 from 13,863 admissions since its Aug. 19 rollout.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $16.1 million, down from last week’s $22.3 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Outmuscles ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ to Hold Top Spot

title: ‘An Oak Tree’ Casts Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan for London Run (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled the first wave of guest performers joining Tim Crouch’s “An Oak Tree” for its run at The Other Palace in Lo
body:
Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled the first wave of guest performers joining Tim Crouch’s “An Oak Tree” for its run at The Other Palace in London, with Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan, Bessie Carter, Rosalie Craig, Hammed Animashaun, George Fouracres, Clare Perkins and Tom Mothersdale each taking on a single performance.

	Crouch performs alongside a different second actor at every show, none of whom read or rehearse the script in advance. “An Oak Tree” runs at The Other Palace from Oct. 7 through Nov. 15.
	

	The schedule of guest performers, in order, runs as follows: Craig on Oct. 9, Perkins on Oct. 13, Mothersdale on Oct. 14, Whelan on Oct. 15, Carter on Oct. 16, Dhawan on Oct. 23, Animashaun on Oct. 29 and Fouracres on Nov. 10.


	Craig recently starred as Kitty Eckersley in Sally Wainwright’s “Riot Women” for BBC One and earned an Olivier nomination for “The Light Princess” at the National Theatre. Perkins appeared in Indhu Rubasingham’s “Bacchae” at the National Theatre and starred opposite Sadie Sink in “Romeo & Juliet” in the West End. Mothersdale’s stage credits include “A Doll’s House” and “Oil” at the Almeida Theatre, while his television work spans “Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light” and “Peaky Blinders.”

	Whelan is known for playing Yara Greyjoy in HBO’s “Game of Thrones” and has appeared across all three series of ITV’s “The Tower.” Carter currently plays Nancy Mitford in BritBox’s “Outrageous” and is also known for playing Prudence Featherington in Netflix’s “Bridgerton.” Dhawan has been announced for Netflix’s “Extraction” and plays the latest incarnation of the Master in BBC One’s “Doctor Who.” Animashaun, a BAFTA nominee for “Black Ops,” appeared in Sky’s “SNL U.K.” and the Donmar Warehouse’s “Dealer’s Choice.” Fouracres, another “SNL U.K.” cast member, is a regular at Shakespeare’s Globe, with credits including “Hamlet” and “Twelfth Night.”
	

	“An Oak Tree” premiered in 2005 and has since been performed hundreds of times across more than 19 countries, with more than 350 guest artists taking part over two decades. Past performers include Frances McDormand, Geoffrey Rush, Peter Dinklage, David Tennant, Jessie Buckley and Phoebe Waller-Bridge.

	The production is part of a new Francesca Moody Productions season at The Other Palace running from Oct. 5, 2026 through Jan. 10, 2027, bringing together three shows that originated at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. The season also includes “Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,” created by Damien Warren-Smith and running Oct. 22 through Jan. 3 with a press night of Oct. 23, and “Feeling Afraid As If Something Terrible Is Going to Happen,” written by Marcelo Dos Santos and starring Steven Webb, running Nov. 19 through Jan. 10.

	Francesca Moody, the season’s executive producer, originated two of the past decade’s most successful television adaptations, “Fleabag” and “Baby Reindeer,” both of which began as stage productions before moving to the screen.

schema.headline: ‘An Oak Tree’ Casts Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan for London Run (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Deauville American Film Festival Reveals Industry Lineup
description:
The Deauville American Film Festival has revealed the lineup for the industry section of its 2026 edition. 

	The Deauville Industry Days sidebar, t
body:
The Deauville American Film Festival has revealed the lineup for the industry section of its 2026 edition. 

	The Deauville Industry Days sidebar, taking place over two days at the festival being held at the French seaside town, will incorporate various talks, panels and sessions. 

	Among them are ‘The Art and Craft of Foodstyling,’ about cinematic food stying for TV and film and featuring the Paris-based culinary design and food styling studio Wallace Food Stylist, the agency behind the screen gastronomy on “Emily in Paris.”
	

	Meanwhile, DDA’s Carola Ash, Sébastien Cauchon of Cinema Collectors and David Thion Les Films Pelleas will take part in the first of a two-part session entitled ‘How to Maximize Your Award Campaign in the U.S.,’ with Benoit Berthe Siward, CEO of The Animation Showcase, leading the second. 


	Focusing on on-screen talent, the panel ‘How to Break in the U.S. as a French Actor, will see casting director Mathilde Snodgrass, actress Mathilde Ollivier (“Overlord”) and talent agent Raphaelle Danglard discuss how to make waves in Hollywood.  

	Elsewhere, CNC’s Joanna Verner and Celine Leclercq will take part in ‘The Financing Schemes in France’ panel, about tax rebate opportunities for international productions. Rounding out the industry section, the ‘A U.S. Production Shot in France’ session will explore how Netflix’s U.S. rom-com “Champagne Problems,” from Mark Steven Johnson and starring Minka Kelly and Tom Wozniczka, was filmed in France in 2024 with producers David Atrakchi and Boris Mendza.

	The Deauville American Film Festival has already unveiled a buzzy lineup of films screening this year, alongside a heavy assortment of stars set to receive honors. Among those getting awards are Brendan Fraser, Ethan Hawke, Faye Dunaway, Susan Sarandon, Sophie Thatcher and Patrick Schwarzenegger.
	

	The 2026 Deauville American Film Festival will run Sep 4-13.

schema.headline: Deauville American Film Festival Reveals Industry Lineup

title: John Oliver Embarrasses Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Over ‘Godawful’ YouTube Reality Show and ‘Real World’ Past
description:
John Oliver is an outspoken fan of reality TV — but not this former “Real World” star.

	On Sunday’s “Last Week Tonight,” the political pundit took
body:
John Oliver is an outspoken fan of reality TV — but not this former “Real World” star.

	On Sunday’s “Last Week Tonight,” the political pundit took aim squarely at Sean Duffy, President Trump’s Secretary of Transportation and former congressman and “The Real World: Boston” cast member. You see, on Wednesday, Duffy dropped all six episodes of “The Great American Road Trip” to YouTube. Though it bills itself as a reality show celebrating America’s 250th anniversary, its travel and its people, as Oliver pointed out, “It’s basically just an expensively-produced test run of a Duffy family reality show with each episode featuring a bare minimum about travel or America but a ton of manufactured reality-TV drama around the Duffy’s doing stuff like planning a family party or, over the course of several episodes, watching their daughter decide which college she’ll attend.” (Duffy’s wife is Fox News contributor Rachel Campos-Duffy, who he met on MTV’s “Road Rules: All Stars.”)
	

	In a clip from the show that was widely mocked online, while discussing whether his daughter can go to Harvard, Duffy remarked, “If I send you there, I think what happens is they have professionalized figuring out how they can take good, young girls like you and, I think, corrupt their minds.”


	“What the fuck are you talking about?” exclaimed Oliver. “First, this was supposed to be a road trip — why are we still in your kitchen? Second, is there anything less relatable than a family whose conflict is, how do I tell my daughter she can’t go to Harvard because we did too good of a job raising her?”
	

	Duffy claimed that the show was shot over seven months and that no taxpayer money was used; rather, the show was funded by the independent company Great American Road Trip Inc., which listed 17 sponsors, Boeing, Toyota, Shell and United Airlines among them, all companies overseen and regulated by Duffy’s Department of Transportation.

	“That’s not great! The only worse answer to ‘Who paid for this?’ than ‘The American taxpayer’ is ‘a bunch of companies I oversee and regulate,’” cracked Oliver.

	And, when Duffy was pressed about the conflict of interest in Congress, he replied, “Don’t you want to celebrate America?” adding, “It’s our birthday!”

	“It’s our birthday? You sound like a fucking child!” exclaimed Oliver. “You do get that just because it’s America’s birthday doesn’t mean you get to do an ethics violation, right? Grow up, Sean!”

	The show was supposed to come out in June but Duffy said it needed to be re-edited so it abided by ethics rules. And Duffy, of course, is a reality-TV veteran.

	“[Duffy] has long loved being on camera. He was actually on ‘The Real World: Boston’ in the late-90s, where he presented himself as deeply horny,” explained Oliver. “In his audition, he reportedly said that he wanted to be on the show because of his interest in ‘cute girls,’ and when asked by a producer how many times he’d had sex in the last six months, he — and I’m quoting here — flashed a big smile and said, ‘Three times. Three different individuals, yeah. And three different times,’ adding, ‘I’m sort of starving right now, guys.’”

	Cue Oliver: “And I’ve got to say: I had sex with three different women, none of whom were interested in an encore, says a lot more about you than I think you wanted to reveal there.”

	What’s worse, during his time on “The Real World: Boston,” Duffy “got attention for annoying the fuck out of his Black castmate Kameelah, who he fought with over affirmative action, complaining he would have gotten into a better college ‘if I were a Black male,’ and at another point, ‘compared [her] to Adolf Hitler while accusing her of reverse racism,’” Oliver offered.  

	As for “The Great American Road Trip,” its YouTube views are dwindling in the thousands and its YouTube page has less than 3K subscribers at time of writing.
	

	“Everyone involved in ‘The Great American Road Trip’ seems like they’d rather sweep it under the rug,” Oliver maintained. “Since it came out, the Duffy’s have barely promoted the show and the Department of Transportation hasn’t posted about it at all… But even if everyone involved wants to move on and act like it never happened, I’m not sure the rest of us should, because the appearance of a conflict of interest here is not going to go away.”

	Oliver then cited how the Department of Transportation has two open investigations into Waymo, which is featured in the series, including for striking a child in the vicinity of a school.

	“Having watched all three hours of this godawful show, from gender reveals to the Duffy’s renewing their vows for no clear reason, it feels less like the country’s been taken on a road trip by Sean Duffy and a lot more like we’ve all been taken for a fucking ride,” he concluded.

schema.headline: John Oliver Embarrasses Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Over ‘Godawful’ YouTube Reality Show and ‘Real World’ Past

title: Erik Poppe Talks Haugesund Opener ‘Beloved,’ Written by Nobel Prize Winner Jon Fosse: ‘People Long for Something Honest and Truthful’
description:
In “Beloved,” opening the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund, Erik Poppe takes on a script by Nobel Prize winner Jon Fosse.

	“It’s a p
body:
In “Beloved,” opening the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund, Erik Poppe takes on a script by Nobel Prize winner Jon Fosse.

	“It’s a project that has been on my desk for many, many years. Jon Fosse wrote it almost 20 years ago. After he received the Nobel Prize in Literature [in 2023], it felt like the whole world wanted to read it. But I always knew it was a powerful piece of work,” he tells Variety. 
	

	“Beloved” follows a couple who meet in a small coastal town. They have a child, but Asle is drawn back to the sea while Gerd remains in the village.


	The film, starring Leo Magnus de la Nuez and Kristi-Helene Giæver Engeberg, was produced by Paradox and SF Production. It’s sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. 

	One of Norway’s most acclaimed directors, Poppe is known for larger productions, from “The King’s Choice” to “Utøya: July 22,” “The Emigrants” and “Quisling: The Final Days.” But focusing on a more intimate story felt right this time.

	“Looking at the world as it is right now, I needed to hold onto some sense of hope – or at least something more human. I wanted to explore the relationship between two people, as well as between a father and son, because it’s a story of daily life I can relate to.” 

	He adds: “We’ve all seen how well they perform in the cinemas, surprisingly enough. People long for something honest and truthful that they can just dive into.”

	The fact that Fosse is only growing in stature doesn’t hurt either. 

	“He’s about to be named one of the most important living authors in the world today, and this isn’t based on his novels or plays. [The screenplay] is an original piece of work that he wrote with only one goal in mind: to make it into a movie.”
	

	Still more adaptations are likely on their way. 

	“I’m quite sure more movies will be made from his novels. As a filmmaker, he’s opening up the space between the dialogue for me to fill in. His style is so simple yet deep. You connect with it, understand it, and it hits you right in the stomach. His novels are short, but when you read them, it feels like Dostoyevsky. I find it extraordinary.” 

	Despite following only two characters and their son, Poppe didn’t change his approach to working with actors.

	“On all my movies, I insist on having at least eight or 12 weeks with them [prior to the shoot]. If I can establish a truthful, honest relationship with my actors, I can push them quite far,” he says. He also paid extra attention to their surroundings. 

	“I spent a lot of time figuring out where to shoot this film. It’s almost like a mythical landscape, a mythical part of Norway. It’s the fourth character in the film.”

	Misty and melancholic, it mirrors their insecurities and growing estrangement. 

	“It’s quite typical of many relationships. It’s so hard to talk to each other,” says Poppe.

	“I was raised by two parents who were almost exactly like these two. Except, it was my mother who left and my sister and I stayed home with my father. The film is about the language these two used to share, which is disappearing, it’s about where they are and what they’re longing for.”

	Which is why, despite that title, there is a darker side to ‘Beloved.’

	“Based on our first screenings, people have been surprised, but they also really love that it’s not your regular love story,” he admits. 

	“I think it’s a brave piece of work by Jon. I was tempted by the fact that he doesn’t follow the paths we are so used to. I wanted to explore how that could work in a movie.”

schema.headline: Erik Poppe Talks Haugesund Opener ‘Beloved,’ Written by Nobel Prize Winner Jon Fosse: ‘People Long for Something Honest and Truthful’

title: ‘Game of Thrones’ Star Kristofer Hivju Turns to Rom-Com With ‘True Love’ by ‘Little Did I Know’s’ Martina Haag (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Norwegian star actor Kristofer Hivju (“Game of Thrones,” “Red One”, “Beck”) will play opposite Frida Hallgren (from Oscar-nominated “As It Is in Hea
body:
Norwegian star actor Kristofer Hivju (“Game of Thrones,” “Red One”, “Beck”) will play opposite Frida Hallgren (from Oscar-nominated “As It Is in Heaven”) in the upcoming Swedish-Croatian rom-com “True Love” (working title). 

	Helmed by actor-turned writer, director and best-selling author Martina Haag, the SF Studios project, now in pre-production, will be pitched Aug. 26. at Haugesund’s Nordic Co-Production Market.
	

	“True Love” marks Haag’s second collaboration with seasoned screenwriter Peter Arrhenius (“Clark,” “Welcome to Sweden,” “Beck”) after the seasoned actor’s directorial debut “Little Did I Know,” which landed a Best Film Award at the Monte-Carlo Television Festival in 2024 before turning into one of Sweden’s biggest box office draws of 2025.


	As with ‘Little Did I know,” “True Love”’s starting point is deceit and divorce and how to bounce back when you’re over 50. 

	According to the logline, when Ellinor (played by Hallgren) is dumped by her husband after 20 years of marriage, she loses faith in life. 

	When she wins €40 million ($46 million) immediately after, she finds it even harder to trust anyone. But then she meets Henrik (Hivju). The latter grew up at the elite Lundsberg boarding school, where his mother worked as a cleaner. To fit in, he learned to lie, and became an irresistibly charming master of deception. Their relationship should never work, but what if they’re exactly what the other needs?“As both main characters are flawed and a bit extreme in the beginning of the film, it was important for us to find great actors that are warm and relatable: Real people in exaggerated situations, that we want to be with and see get better,” said Hivju and Hallgren Haag. 
	

	They added: “Both Frida and Kristofer feel grounded and are capable of going from being extremely funny to super sensitive. And of course, the chemistry and dynamics between the actors is super important in a romantic comedy. If the spark isn’t there, it doesn’t matter how great the story is. We’re so happy to have Frida and Kristofer on board!”

	Added SF Studios producer Helen Ahlsson: “Frida is a wonderfully warm and talented actress, and one audiences have taken to their hearts over the years. Kristofer has never really played a romantic lead before, which was perhaps a new challenge he was very keen to take on. In this film, you’ll discover a new Hivju like you’ve never seen before,” she enthusiastically shared with Variety.

	Haag said catering for mature audiences came naturally. “I love stories about and for women – and men – over 50,” she said. “I really can’t understand why we don’t see more of them as a whole scope of relatable, life altering relationship questions appear after surviving Project Family and raising the kids. One being deceit and divorce –  as in “Little Did I Know” – but also how to be able to trust and love again.”

	“This story is about that,” she added. “Who we were, who we are, who we try to present ourself as, and who we really want to be. How can anyone dare to let their guard down and risk being hurt once again? We take that premise to the extreme in this film.”

	Teaming up again with Arrhenius was a no-brainer. 

	“It is rare to find a writing partner that both has a skillset that completes your own and at the same time can respect and see your own strengths, like the yin and the yang,” she said, pointing out that “Peter is very interested in structure and serves up a lot of drastic jokes and situations, while I tend to focus on grounding these ideas in character and ”what would a real person do in this situation.”

	“When that works, what you get is drastic, funny situations happening to characters that feels true. Real emotions without being kitchen-sink drama. We share that desire to both touch an audience, but in an entertaining way,” she observed. 

	Seasoned producer Ahlsson who’s worked mostly on dramas for film and TV – from Alicia Vikander’s Swedish debut “Pure” to Rojda Sekersöz’s upcoming “Will You Care if I Die” –  said she couldn’t resist boarding her first rom-com after reading the script.
	

	“It’s got the magic of British comedy hits such as “Bridget Jones’s Diary” or “Mamma Mia,” which balance believable, engaging characters with lightness, humor and emotions. It’s a tricky mix that you can’t take lightly,” she said.

	Filming between Sweden-Stockholm, Dalecarlia-and Croatia is due to start Oct. 8, with delivery pencilled for fall 2027.

	The feature is produced by Scandi giant SF Studios in co-production with Croatia’s Kinorama, SVT and NRK, with funding from the Swedish Film Institute, Film Stockholm, Film i Dalarna, and a Croatian tax rebate.

	Ahlsson said she will discuss global sales at the New Nordic Films market unspooling Aug. 25-28 at Haugesund, Norway.

title: Foo Fighters and Gustavo Dudamel Blow Up the Hollywood Bowl as Conductor Blows Out the Candle on His Time With the LA Phil: Concert Review
description:
The LA Phil has played with plenty of pop and rock acts before, but it may have taken Foo Fighters to really put the dude in Dudamel. 

	And not a m
body:
The LA Phil has played with plenty of pop and rock acts before, but it may have taken Foo Fighters to really put the dude in Dudamel. 

	And not a moment too soon, with this being famed conductor Gustavo Dudamel‘s final weekend at the helm of Los Angeles’ primary house symphony. The Phil’s hookup with Dave Grohl and company Saturday night was the middle act in a three-night local finale for Dudamel — a delectable dip into what old-school symphony buffs would once have considered low culture. The entire weekend, though, was about asking Beethoven to roll over, as it were, for some of the maestro’s less classical loves. The Foos collab was sandwiched in between Friday and Sunday concerts where the focus was on acknowledging Dudamel’s connections to Latin American and specifically Venezuelan music.
	

	Understandably, Grohl had to make it at least a little about himself, too, or more to the point, this being a milestone for his 32-year-old band. “ This is a first,” he told the sold-out crowd at the outset. “First of all, I don’t know if you know, but Foo Fighters has never played the Hollywood Bowl before… Usually in this part of the program I ask the audience if they love rock ‘n’ roll music… But tonight, i’m gonna ask this question for the first time: Do you love Dudamel? Me too. so let’s play some rock ‘n’ roll for Mr. Dudamel. That’s what we came here to do.”


	For a while, it seemed as if this show might really mark a serious first: Grohl, who tends to pepper his stage banter with the F-word at least once in every sentence — used as an exclamation, adjective, adverb, noun, verb and preposition — seemed to be inspired by the occasion, and by the presence of dozens of the world’s finest musicians in formalwear, to be deliberately abstaining from profanity. But if that was indeed a goal, finally, toward the end, he couldn’t help himself. “Ladies and gentlemen, on an evening like tonight, I don’t really know how to say goodbye, because I wish that we could do this every fucking night for the rest of our lives with all of these amazing people.”
	



	A quick, unscientific survey of Foo fans suggested that not one of them would have a problem with that (in, you know, the theoretical world where Grohl could outspend and out-prestige the New York Philharmonic, where Dudamel is headed next). Fans online — those who’d been at the concert and those just tracking it from afar — immediately began clamoring for a commercial release of Saturday’s show. That desire was well-justified. When some bands do symphonic hook-ups, it makes for a satisfying experiment, but not necessarily one you need to hear endlessly. The arrangements here were so well-balanced, and so in keeping with what made these tracks feel as dramatic as they did in the first place, that you could imagine recordings from the show taking the place of the originals in some fans’ streaming playlists, indefinitely if not for all time.

	Some artists who do Bowl shows with the LA Phil or its sister symphony, the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra, run through something close to their normal set and require whoever is assigned to do the orchestrations to follow suit. Fortunately, Grohl took a broader view of what catalog material might benefit most from the augmentation, even if it meant narrowing down the length of the setlist, since orchestral players by definition don’t work rock ‘n’ roll hours.

	“Listen, tonight we’re gonna play as many things as we can before we have to stop,” the singer said early in the hour-and-40-minutes performance. “You know, we usually play for three hours a night. But tonight, we picked the best songs that we could perform with our friends in the LA Phil and Mr. Gustavo Dudamel. Some of these you may have never heard before. So sit back and enjoy a song called ‘A320.'”



	

					Foo Fighters and Gustavo Dudamel (third from left) take a bow at the close of Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA, at the Hollywood Bowl August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Now, pretty much the only people who’ve been holding out for “A320” to rejoin the Foos’ set after a quarter-century of absence are the half-dozen people still clutching to their CDs of the 1998 “Godzilla” soundtrack, where it first lived and kind of died a quiet death. But, as one of the rare songs to have included string arrangements on the original record, it was prime territory for revival here. (And the band has also been trying it out at a few non-orchestral tour stops this year, maybe with the thought of getting it ready for the Bowl.) As on the age-old original, the first half of the six-minute track was sweeping in its use of orchestral augmentation, and then the second half put aside both strings and vocals to turn into a pure band jam. That’s counterintuitive, since it would be more common to start a song without orchestration and then add it in, rather than the reverse. But the band fury is as climactic as anything that could be done continuing to have the full ensemble play… and Dudamel looked happy enough to put his baton down, turn around and just watch the group play for a few minutes. (The Phil was present at points on every one of the 15 songs song, but there were plenty of stretches within those songs where they took five.)
	



	

					HB26 Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	The band’s most faithful followers may be happy to hear “Times Like These” played for the 894th time (according to setlist.fm), but having “A320” come into the set early was a sign that this would really be a night to make the hardcore happy. And there ended up being three more rarities to set fans aflutter: “I Should Have Known,” being played live for the first time since 2012; “Razor,” being performed for the first time since 2006; and “Home,” getting a live airing for the first time since 2007 (and only the fifth performance overall). What these surprise additions meant, in human terms, is that Grohl understood the assignment, when it came to joining forces with another powerful institution: you find the songs that have been waiting for that moment.

	Of course, he also considered some of the band’s greatest hits to be in that category. “This was made for the Hollywood Bowl, I think,” Grohl said, prefacing “My Hero.” It was hard to argue with that assessment, when the song took on a healthy dose of brass that sounded noble enough for a military funeral… not to mention a surprise solo harp for just a few seconds when the rest of the onstage complement dropped out for a dramatic pause. 

	But it really was some of the lesser known or slightly less celebrated songs making bigger impressions. A choir came out on two songs in the middle of the set, both of them highlights. First among them was “The Sky Is a Neighborhood” (the title of which lets you know that Grohl does have a poetic side, however much his stage banter falls into the category of basic-bitch). The frontman did some of his punkiest scream-singing of the night, content to know that the dozen or so berobed figures surrounding him could keep up the melodious quotient of the tune; Chris Shiflett turned in a short, sweet and rare guitar solo over some of that choral wailing, as the band thunderously pounded it out in 6/8 time. Maximalism doesn’t come much more maximal than that, and it was genuinely musical as well as bombastic. 



	

					HB26 Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Then, taking it way down, members of the participating YOLA (the Youth Orchestra of Los Angeles), identifiable by their shirts (and by their, duh, youth), did a somber string opening for “Run,” replicating or replacing the studio version’s extended acoustic guitar intro, before the rock and the choir kicked in — another certain highlight, despite the tune not being on the list of internationally approved classics.
	

	More expected standouts included “Aurora,” which Grohl has been faithfully dedicating nightly to Taylor Hawkins, with the orchestra again going silent during the final stretch so that the core band could use the hypnotically interesting riffage to send a former comrade into the afterlife with 17,000 phones aglow. 

	It didn’t seem as if it would get much more sentimental than that, yet it did, as the unlikely penultimate pick turned out to be “Home,” of which Grohl said, “We’ve only done this song once.” (He was off-count by about three instances, according to the online stats, but close enough.) Taking a stool for the most sedate of his ballads, Grohl explained that he was never previously able to get through the 2007 song “because it’s such a meaningful song to me that whenever I heard it, I couldn’t stop from crying. And whenever we played it, there’s no way I could make it through the entire song without just bursting into tears. But what I’ve found is that while you’re singing it, if you think of other things, you can actually make it to the end without crying.” There was a pause, while the audience waited for Grohl to explain if he was picturing the audience naked, or something. “I’m not gonna tell you what I was thinking about,” he then announced. “But we got to the end of the fucking song, so there you go.”

	There might have been other reasons to wonder whether Grohl would make it through the set, early on — like, right, at the very beginning, when the set started with a slow and stark couple of verses of “Times Like These,” and the singer’s voice cracked when he sang that high, introductory “I…” And the same thing happened when that note came around again. Was it an inauspicious way to start the set, revealing a voice that was tour-ravaged… or was Grohl faking us out with some exaggerated emotion? Whichever was the case, he quickly rallied, or otherwise revved up to speed, and there were no worries about whether his howl would survive this hot night from then on. But he had us going for about half a minute there. 

	A good thing he turned out to deceptively be in top shape after all; this will go down in many fans’ books as one of the group’s all-timers. Whether the show is memorialized through some sort of commemorative recording or just cameraphone videos, it’s some of the little things that stick in memory, at least initially: the way that the horns filled in the space between the lines of verses on “All My Life” with frenetic stabs, or how, on “Learn to Fly,” the strings played slightly off the beat in the dramatic coda, versus the straightforward slamming of the band. And the fake endings … so many fake endings. But Grohl is showman enough to know: when a fast song leaves ’em wanting more, it doesn’t hurt to seem to quit and then actually give a little more.
	

	Dudamel did not do much talking; if he has any sentimental feelings he wants to share with the L.A. audience about taking leave of them, presumably he will do it during Sunday night’s true swan song. But he did speak while introducing what amounted to the evening’s opening act — a 15-minute border-crossing suite, composer Aldemaro Romero’s “Fuga con Pajarillo,” which segued back and forth between the full orchestra and Venezuelan musicians, including Eduardo Betancourt, Jorge Glem and Moisés Torrealba. The main reason for the night was, as Grohl said, “to give Gustavo one more big rock show before he has to leave this wonderful city.” But even then, he couldn’t leave Venezuela out of it. New York will be blessed to have someone so faithful to his truest loves.

	Which definitely do include rock. Dudamel’s performance conducting with Foo Fighters Saturday made you wish the LA Phil, or future employers, would dedicate one of the venue’s big screens solely to a Gustavo Cam, so everyone could see how headbanging really should look, when it’s being done by a pro.



	

					Dave Grohl and conductor Gustavo Dudamel perform as part of Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Setlist for Foo Fighters with the LA Phil, Gustavo Dudamel and YOLA at the Hollywood Bowl, August 22, 2026:Times Like These All My LifeThe PretenderWalkA320 My HeroLearn to FlyThe Sky Is a NeighborhoodRunI Should Have KnownRazor AuroraBest of YouHomeEverlong



	

					Gustvavo Dudamel with Venezuelan musicians backstage at Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic

title: Bret Michaels Shares Health Update After Canceling Rest of 2026 Tour
description:
Bret Michaels
                          Comeback Show Was Too Much Too Soon
body:
Bret Michaels
                          Comeback Show Was Too Much Too Soon
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Bret Michaels says his body may be forcing him to slow down ... but his mind is still very much onstage.
      
    
            The Poison frontman gave fans a fresh health update Sunday after canceling the rest of his 2026 tour ... saying he's been working closely with doctors and physical therapists following his attempted comeback Friday in Sugar Hill, Georgia.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Bret says he thought he could power through his recent health issues ... but admits he didn't fully account for the Atlanta heat, a coast-to-coast flight and new medication adjustments.
      

            He is a Type 1 diabetic and says all of that took a toll on his blood sugar and blood pressure ... and now his doctors are tweaking his meds and insulin.
      
    
            Still, Bret says he's itching to get back out there ... writing, "If I could, I would be back out there tomorrow."
      
    
            Bret's team announced Saturday he was canceling the rest of his 2026 shows after doctors and paramedics checked him out following Friday night's concert ... determining he needed more time to recover from recent surgeries.
      
    
            Bret says he was especially crushed to miss Tennessee's Mountain Music Festival ... but vowed to return in 2027 or 2028.
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            For now ... he's hoping this latest setback is temporary.

Simon Cowell
                          Missing 'AGT' For Weeks ...
                          Due to Routine Surgery

                              August 23, 2026
                            8:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Simon Cowell is going to be missing from "America's Got Talent" for the next couple of weeks while he undergoes a routine procedure related to his back, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Cowell is scheduled to have back surgery soon, and the procedure will force him to sit out several weeks of the hit NBC show.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told this is a routine procedure and there is no indication of a new major health crisis. Cowell has a history of back issues following a serious electric-bike accident in 2020 that required surgery.
      

            It's unclear who will fill in for Cowell during his absence or exactly when he'll return to the judges' table.
      
    
            The 66-year-old British music mogul and TV personality is best known for his brutally honest judging style on "American Idol," "The X Factor" and "America’s Got Talent."
      
    
            Cowell has also been instrumental in creating and developing major acts including One Direction and Fifth Harmony, cementing his reputation as one of pop music’s most influential talent scouts.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            We recently caught up with Cowell in March, when he weighed in on Tom Sandoval and his band ... saying he didn’t see them as major record sellers but thought they could make serious money playing weddings and parties.
      
    
            Cowell also revealed to us he’s considering putting together another boy or girl group, saying he’s still looking for the next big act.
      
    
            We’ve reached out to Crowell’s reps for comment. So far, no word back.
